samples.text:
Nowadays, many big international companies are building factories and offices in developing countries. This has both advantages and disadvantages for the local people. In my opinion, the advantages are more important.

The biggest advantage is jobs. When a foreign company open a factory, it needs hundreds of workers, so many people who was unemployed can get a job and earn a regular salary. This helps families to pay for food, education and health care. Also, international companies often pay higher wages than local companies. Another advantage is that workers can learn new skills and technology. For example, if an employee works in a car factory, he can learn how to use modern machines, and later he can use this knowledge in other jobs. Moreover, the government gets more money from taxes, which it can spend on roads and schools.

However, there are also some disadvantages. Some companies pay very low salary and the working conditions are bad, for example people work for long hours without enough rest. In addition, the factories can cause pollution to the rivers and air, and this is harmful for the people's health who live nearby. Finally, the most of the profit goes back to the company's home country, so the developing country does not get all the benefit.

In conclusion, international companies bring both good and bad effects to developing countries. They create jobs and teach new skills, but they can also cause pollution and pay low wages. I believe that the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, but the government should make strict rules to protect workers and the environment.
samples.why: Addresses both sides with a clear judgement · relevant ideas, some supported by simple examples, others underdeveloped · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · several agreement and article errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
In recent decades, multinational corporations have moved a growing share of their manufacturing and service operations to developing nations. While this trend can create problems for local communities, I believe that, overall, the benefits for ordinary people in these countries are greater than the costs.

The most obvious advantage is employment. Foreign firms often create thousands of jobs in regions where work is scarce, giving people a steady income and the chance to escape poverty. These jobs frequently pay more than local alternatives, and they may come with training that local employers cannot afford to provide. Over time, employees gain technical and managerial skills which they can take to other companies or use to start their own businesses. In addition, the presence of large international firms tends to improve local infrastructure, as roads, ports and power supplies are upgraded to serve them.

On the other hand, there are serious disadvantages. Some corporations are attracted mainly by cheap labour and weak regulations, and as a result workers may face long hours, low pay and unsafe conditions. Environmental damage is another concern, since factories can pollute rivers and air in countries where laws are poorly enforced. Furthermore, large foreign companies can drive small local businesses out of the market, and a significant part of the profits is sent back abroad rather than reinvested locally.

However, these negative effects are not unavoidable. When governments set and enforce minimum standards for wages, safety and pollution, foreign investment can bring benefits without the worst forms of exploitation.

In conclusion, although multinational companies can exploit workers and damage the environment, the jobs, skills and infrastructure they bring represent a major opportunity for people in developing countries. For this reason, I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, provided that effective regulation are in place.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both sides developed with relevant support, though some points are generalised · clear paragraph topics · good range of vocabulary (scarce, exploitation) · mostly accurate, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The relocation of factories and offices by multinational corporations to lower-income countries is one of the defining features of the global economy. Its impact on local populations is mixed, but I would contend that, where host governments regulate effectively, the advantages for ordinary citizens outweigh the disadvantages.

The most immediate gain is employment. In economies with high levels of informal or subsistence work, a job with a foreign firm often provides the first regular wage a household has received, together with a degree of stability that enables families to plan, save and invest in their children's education. Beyond income, these positions frequently involve formal training, exposing workers to modern production methods, management practices and quality standards. Such knowledge rarely stays within one company; it spreads as employees move on or establish suppliers of their own, gradually raising the productivity of the wider economy. Foreign investment can also stimulate improvements in transport and energy that benefit the whole population.

The costs, however, can be severe. Some corporations deliberately seek out countries with lax labour and environmental laws, and the consequences can include excessive working hours, dangerous workplaces and serious contamination of land and water. There is also the risk of dependency: an economy built around foreign-owned plants is vulnerable if a company decides to relocate again in search of even cheaper costs, leaving entire towns without work. Moreover, much of the value generated flows back to shareholders overseas rather than being reinvested locally.

Importantly, these harms are largely a function of governance rather than of foreign investment itself. Countries that enforce labour rights, require environmental safeguards and encourage links with domestic suppliers tend to capture far more of the benefits.

In conclusion, multinational investment carries real risks of exploitation and instability, yet the jobs, skills and infrastructure it brings can transform living standards. On balance, and with sound regulation, its advantages for local people outweigh its disadvantages.
samples.why: Sufficiently addresses the question with a nuanced, clearly argued judgement · ideas extended and logically linked · cohesion well managed · wide, precise vocabulary used naturally · wide range of accurate complex structures.
